title: The Double-Edged Nature of the Rashomon Set for Trustworthy Machine Learning
claim: Increasing diversity among near-optimal models improves robustness but worsens privacy, exposing a trade-off between the two trustworthiness goals.
layout: single scatter plot with colorbar on right, color encodes model count
description: A single scatter plot with reconstruction error on the x-axis (about 0.0 to 0.2) and adversarial accuracy on the y-axis (0 to 0.5). Each dot is a Rashomon set of a given size. A colorbar on the right is labeled 'Number of Models' and runs from dark gray-purple (small sets, about 1) through magenta and orange to pale cream (200). Dark points with few models sit low and to the right, spread along a steep downward diagonal. The lowest point has reconstruction error about 0.21 and accuracy near 0. Brighter points with many models cluster in the top-left corner near accuracy 0.5 and error under 0.03. The eye goes first to the bright cluster in the top-left, then follows the dark trail down to the lower right. There is no 'ours' label or annotation.
caption: The robustness–privacy trade-off on the COMPAS dataset: with the increasing diversity in the Rashomon set, adversarial accuracy increases (greater reactive robustness), while reconstruction error decreases (greater information leakage).
abstract: Real-world machine learning (ML) pipelines rarely produce a single model; instead, they produce a Rashomon set of many near-optimal ones. We show that this multiplicity reshapes key aspects of trustworthiness. At the individual-model level, sparse interpretable models tend to preserve privacy but are fragile to adversarial attacks. In contrast, the diversity within a large Rashomon set enables reactive robustness: even when an attack compromises one model, a practitioner can switch to a different near-optimal model that remains accurate, without retraining. However, the same diversity increases information leakage, as disclosing more near-optimal models provides an attacker with progressively richer views of the training data. This produces a robustness-privacy trade-off governed by diversity, which we analyze theoretically and empirically. Beyond this trade-off, Rashomon sets are stable under small distribution shifts, so a set computed once remains valid under such shifts without re-computation. Our results highlight the dual role of Rashomon sets as both a resource and a risk for trustworthy ML.
